summary: Tip-Top House on Mount Moosilauke, a summit building used in the White Mountains' early lookout network; burned 1942; foundation stones remain.

facts.design: Summit building (Tip-Top House) used as a lookout site

access.note: Trails cross the mountain and reach the summit. The summit was donated to Dartmouth College in 1920, and the College owns just under 4,600 acres of the mountain.

corrections.why: Foundation stones of the Tip Top House remain on the summit, which fits the 'ruins' category (remains only) better than 'gone'.
NH Family Hikes files Moosilauke among ground-level lookout stations, and the sources describe a summit building used as a lookout site. None of the sources read describes a cab on a roof.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Dartmouth exhibit says a presumed lightning strike burned the Tip Top House in 1942. The Wikipedia Ravine Lodge article says a Dartmouth-run Summit Camp (1920-1942) burned down from a lightning strike. Neither source says whether these are the same building, so the story reports both and does not merge them.

sources.title: Eyes on the Forest: White Mountain Fire Lookout Tower History

notes_for_editor: The state's lookout history PDF was not readable (HTTP 403), so the lookout years at the summit are not confirmed. A search summary put the station's end soon after 1913; that claim was not verified from a fetched page and is left out. Whether the lookout operated from the Tip Top House itself is inferred from the whitemountainhistory and NH Family Hikes sources, not stated directly. The 'rooftop' kind correction is proposed on the basis of the NH Family Hikes grouping and the absence of any roof-cab description; FFLA types the site 'Hotel', which the pipeline maps to rooftop, so the editor should confirm before accepting. The 1942 loss is reported two ways (see resolved_conflicts). The Ravine Lodge article's 1920 date for the Summit Camp is taken from Wikipedia only. The story no longer calls the summit a 'rather than towers' site, because no source states that. The 1920 donation and the Summit Camp years were added to events so the timeline matches the story. The record has no photos for this site.
